Attention: You can't notice everything, so attention is selective. That's why you can miss a change (change blindness) or an object right in front of you (inattentional blindness), yet still hear your name across a noisy room (cocktail party effect) or spot the one odd item (pop-out).
Top-down vs. bottom-up: Bottom-up processing starts with the senses sending information up to the brain (sensation). Top-down processing uses knowledge, experience and context to interpret it (perception), as when you read messy handwriting or scrambled words.
Thresholds: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus you can detect half the time. The difference threshold is the smallest change you notice half the time. Weber's law says that change is a constant percentage, not a constant amount.
Extrasensory perception: ESP claims include telepathy, clairvoyance and precognition. There is no scientific basis for it; psychics do no better than guesses, and they seem accurate because people remember the hits and forget the misses.
